summary: When Pharisees from Jerusalem fault His disciples for eating with unwashed hands, Jesus exposes their traditions and teaches that defilement comes from the heart.
key_insight: The Pharisees asked about hands; Jesus answered about hearts. Their washings dealt with what touches a person from outside, but every item on His list of what defiles, beginning with “evil thoughts,” starts on the inside, where no washing reaches.
story: Pharisees and scribes came from Jerusalem to Jesus. They saw some of His disciples eating bread with unwashed hands. The Pharisees, and indeed all the Jews, would not eat without washing their hands in a special way, keeping the tradition of the elders, and they also washed cups, pitchers and copper vessels. {Mk} So they asked Him, “Why do Your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.” {Mt}

Jesus answered, “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition?” {Mt} God had commanded His people to honor father and mother. But they taught that a man could declare his support for his parents “Corban,” that is, a gift to God, and then no longer use it to help them. {Mk} “Thus you have made the commandment of God of no effect by your tradition.” {Mt}
“Hypocrites!” He said. Isaiah had described them well: “These people draw near to Me with their mouth, And honor Me with their lips, But their heart is far from Me.” {Mt}

Then Jesus called the crowd to Himself. “Hear Me, everyone, and understand: There is nothing that enters a man from outside which can defile him; but the things which come out of him, those are the things that defile a man.” {Mk}

His disciples came and told Him, “Do You know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” Jesus answered that every plant His heavenly Father had not planted would be uprooted. “Let them alone. They are blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind leads the blind, both will fall into a ditch.” {Mt}

Back in the house, away from the crowd, {Mk} Peter asked Him to explain the parable. {Mt} “Are you thus without understanding also?” Jesus said. Food enters the stomach, not the heart, and passes out of the body, “thus purifying all foods.” Then He said, “For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lewdness, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within and defile a man.” {Mk}
differences: Mark explains the Jewish washing customs for his readers; Matthew does not.
Matthew gives Jesus’ answer about the commandment first and the quotation from Isaiah second; Mark gives Isaiah first.
Matthew writes “God commanded”; Mark writes “Moses said.” Mark keeps the Hebrew word “Corban.”
Only Matthew records the Pharisees’ offense, the uprooted plant and the blind guides, and names Peter as the one who asked.
Only Mark includes “thus purifying all foods,” and his list of evils is longer: thirteen to Matthew’s seven.

scene.label: The tradition of the elders
scene.text: The Pharisees held to a large body of oral rulings handed down by earlier teachers, which they treated as binding alongside the written Law. Around AD 200 much of it was written down in the Mishnah.

scene.label: Washing hands
scene.text: This washing was about religious purity, not hygiene. The Law told priests to wash before their service (Exodus 30:19–21); the Pharisees applied that kind of purity to ordinary meals, especially after contact with the marketplace.

scene.label: Corban
scene.text: “Corban” is the Hebrew word for an offering brought to God. By declaring money or property Corban, a son could put it out of his parents’ reach, and such a vow might still leave him the use of it himself. The fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12) included caring for aging parents.

scene.label: From Jerusalem
scene.text: These scribes and Pharisees had come from the capital, as others had before (Mark 3:22). Opposition to Jesus was no longer local; leaders in Jerusalem were watching Him closely.

witnesses.matthew: Writes for readers who knew Jewish customs, so he does not explain the washings. He includes Jesus’ word about the blind guides and the uprooted plant, and he puts God’s commandment at the front, in keeping with his concern for a righteousness that goes deeper than the scribes and Pharisees (5:20).
witnesses.mark: Explains the washings and translates “Corban” for Gentile readers. Many translations read “thus purifying all foods” as Mark’s own comment that Jesus declared all foods clean; the NKJV keeps the phrase in Jesus’ words. Peter, whose memories likely stand behind Mark, later learned the same lesson on a rooftop in Joppa (Acts 10:9–16).

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks with authority over the traditions of the elders and over what makes a person clean. He sees past clean hands to the heart, and He names plainly what comes out of it.
seeing.living: Jesus’ list leaves no one clean, because it begins with evil thoughts. Religious habits can cover a heart far from God, and even a gift to God can become a way around His commands. Bring Him the heart itself, and let His word, not custom, decide what pleases Him.
seeing.ponder: Where might your devotion to God be serving as a reason not to obey Him?

preaching.big_idea: God looks past clean hands to the heart, where defilement begins.
preaching.watch_for: The word “tradition” appears five times in 7:1–13, set against “the commandment of God” and “the word of God.” Then Jesus turns from the leaders to the crowd (7:14) and to the disciples in the house (7:17), each time speaking more plainly.
